prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, and their development to fractional uncertainties of 10^-18, opening new regimes of precision measurement

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B001 alone, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After reading all eight round-1 statements, the striking fact is that every member now reaches the same configuration, but I do not count that as evidence. What matters to me is the experimental record. The magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift while letting many thousands of atoms be interrogated at once, which trades the signal-to-noise limit of a single ion for a many-atom ensemble, and that is a different measurement principle from the trapped-ion clocks honoured in 2012. Independent laboratories now reproduce uncertainties near 10^-18, compare clocks across sites, and resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres to centimetres. Those cross-comparisons are the experimental check I trust most, because a systematic budget is only credible once a second clock disagrees or agrees with it. The consequences, tighter limits on varying constants and dark-matter couplings and relativistic geodesy, are measured, not promised. For the chair's questions: I would accept B001 as distinct from 2005 and 2012, and I want the citation to name the lattice concept and its realisation, not clocks or precision in general. I do not think the SI second redefinition should delay the prize. A two-name credit is defensible if the citation is scoped to the lattice concept and its first realisation (Katori) and the route to the 10^-18 regime with spin-polarised fermions and many-body control (Ye), and I would welcome the external priority check Danielsson asks for.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains that this can be read as a refinement of the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize that covered ion clocks, and nobody has settled that by argument; I answer it only by pointing to the different principle and the two orders of magnitude gained. A second weakness is attribution: Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley, Campbell and the SYRTE, NIST and PTB groups made decisive contributions, and a two-name credit necessarily leaves them out. I have not verified the priority record for the first strontium lattice clock and the 10^-18 result, and from my own experience I know how easily priority becomes blurred when several groups converge on one scheme. Finally, the largest payoffs (the redefinition of the second, geodesy at scale, dark-matter limits that actually bite) are still ahead, so a sceptic could say the demonstrated new-physics output is modest so far.

responses.point: Olsson worries that the headline 10^-18 result is a record in systematic control, closer to a record than a discovery, and that the case depends on whether the prize is for the original experiment.
responses.response: I think the distinction matters and I would draw it explicitly in the citation. A record in systematic control alone would not meet the bar for me. What qualifies here is the combination: Katori's idea and first realisation, which is an invention, and the demonstration, mostly from Ye's group, that the lattice interactions, blackbody shift and Stark shifts could be understood and controlled well enough that independently built clocks agree. The agreement between laboratories is the evidence that the number reflects physics and not one lab's budget. I also agree with your point that experimental verification is the mandate, and the redshift measurements over millimetres are the nearest thing to nature checking the claim. I would therefore keep the citation anchored on the lattice clock concept and realisation, with 10^-18 as the demonstrated consequence.

responses.point: Danielsson, as Secretary, wants external expert reports to confirm the priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal, and wants the citation to stress the lattice concept over clock accuracy.
responses.response: I support both. The citation should say optical lattice clocks and magic-wavelength trapping, and the priority record for the proposal, the first strontium clock and the first 10^-18 result should be confirmed by external reports before the vote is final, because none of us has verified it independently. I would add a practical request to the reports: separate the proposal, the first demonstration and the long-term evaluation of systematic shifts, and say which groups achieved each step independently. If the reports show that the Paris or NIST/PTB contribution was equal in the decisive step, I would reconsider the two-name credit. Based on what is on the table now, I find Katori and Ye the most defensible pair, and I agree with you that none of the reservations overturns the case.

responses.point: Johansson lists as an open question whether the redefinition of the second should be well advanced before the award, and keeps B003 and B042 as alternatives, recusing himself from B003.
responses.response: On timing, I read the redefinition as a decision by metrologists that rests on the same cross-laboratory comparisons that make the physics credible, so it follows the science and should not gate the prize. If we waited, we would be rewarding a procedural milestone. On the alternatives, I agree with your recusal on B003 and I note my own WACQT overlap with Chalmers, which I would not expect to bias me but which I disclose. I keep B042 and B003 as alternatives for the same reason you do: both are sound but each carries a credit problem, five names for B042 and four for B003, and B003 follows the 2025 prize closely. I would not add either as a second part this year, because a two-part prize that includes a weaker-attributed part dilutes a clean B001 result.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks in the summary whether anyone wants a second part, and earlier ranked B002 second while wanting the redefinition to be well advanced.
responses.response: I do not want a second part, and I will say why in measurement terms. A second prize part should have an experimental case as solid as B001, and none of the alternatives currently has one with a clean allocation to three people. B042 has the most experimental weight: Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger demonstrated the Mott insulator and fermionic many-body physics, while Zoller and Cirac supplied the proposals, but the theory-versus-experiment split cannot be resolved inside three names without choosing arbitrarily. B003 is in the same position with Girvin or Blais as the fourth name, and I would not like to decide that while also compressing the circuit story into one year after 2025. I understand your caution on the timing of the redefinition, but I think the physics is mature now.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B006 and B004 as alternatives and says the credit among topological-insulator theorists is genuinely split.
responses.response: I accept that point for B010 and B004, and it is one reason I do not push them: the Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane-Mele and Hasan lines are intertwined, and Molenkamp's HgTe experiment is only one of several experimental routes, so three names cannot represent it fairly. On B006 I still think the hexatic evidence is system dependent and some melting is first order, as you note, and the 2016 prize overlap is substantial, so I do not rate it as an alternative for the ballot. I would not argue against your elegance criterion, but I want the decisive experimental confirmation to be stronger before such a theory-only credit is considered by us.

uncertainties: Whether the external priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock and the 10^-18 result supports a Katori and Ye pair without other clock groups.
Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, rather than a refinement of them.
How much of the demonstrated 10^-18 performance is attributable to Ye's group versus the other national laboratories, which I cannot judge from the evidence on the table.
Whether a two-part prize adding B042 or B003 would be better than B001 alone once the credit allocation is settled, which I currently doubt.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the credited persons on the shortlist is apparent. I work in atomic physics and quantum optics at Lund and have broad field proximity to B001 and B042, but I have no mentor, co-author or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited names that I know of. Lindroth's disclosed collaboration with Anne L'Huillier is a Lund connection I share only institutionally. My WACQT role at Chalmers overlaps with Johansson's institution, which matters only for superconducting-circuit candidates such as B003, so I would weigh B003 only as an alternative and defer to Johansson's recusal.
